turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, the system's crawling. Give me a tick. What are we doing today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Just a check-up, really. My sister's been on at me for months and I kept putting it off.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): When were you last in?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The possums wrecked the veggie patch, and the tap's leaking, so between that and— oh, the clinic. A year? Bit over, maybe.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): About a year. Anything specific, or a general going-over?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): General, I suppose. Blood pressure's the thing they always bang on about. I've been good with the tablet.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which tablet? Wrong screen. Say that again?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Perindopril. Four milligrams, mornings. I don't miss that one.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else you're taking?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Aspirin, the little white ones. On and off, when I remember. Grandkids were down from Geelong and the week went sideways.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): What dose is the aspirin?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Geelong was lovely, waterfront, fish and chips, the kids were feral by four.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): The dose, sorry. I lost you, the screen's jumped again.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Hundred milligrams, I think. That's what the box says.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain. I walk the dog every morning by the river. Kelpie cross, Pip, pulls like a train.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any shortness of breath?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): The vet can't fit her in till Thursday. Her nails are a disgrace, honestly.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, breathing. Sorry. I'm alright unless I rush, then I'm a bit puffed. I'm sixty-two, I put that down to age.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you on a cholesterol tablet?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Was. Rosuvastatin. I stopped it in March, the muscle aches were shocking.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): What strength was that?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten? Or twenty. Don't remember. They also wrote ezetimibe and I never filled the script, never took it.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): So not the ezetimibe. And the rosuvastatin, you—
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Stopped in March, yeah. Knees have been niggly for years from the gardening, both of them, though I'm not here about that.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Achy with the gardening, comes and goes, been years. Not why I came in, mind you.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Back to the chest. You said there was no pain. What about climbing stairs, or walking fast?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, there's a tight feeling. Not pain exactly. Like a band around the chest. Only on the stairs at home, or if I'm legging it for the bus.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long's that tightness been there?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I can't put a date on it. Maybe a month. Could be longer. I honestly don't know.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it go if you rest?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, a minute or two and it's gone. If I dawdle up the stairs it doesn't come on at all.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sweating with it? Jaw pain, or pain down the arm?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No sweating. Jaw's fine. Arm, no, I don't think so.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Most times you hurry, or just occasionally?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Most times, if I don't take it slow. The 412 is hopeless, you get halfway down George Street and it sails past, so I'm forever—
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again? The chart's flicked over.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Most times when I'm rushing. Not when I go slow. That was it.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I've cut the wine right back. None on weeknights. My husband still has a beer with dinner, that's his business.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Smoking, I meant. Not the wine.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Never have. Can't stand the smell. The wine is one glass on a Saturday if we go out.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any drug allergies?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I'm aware of.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heart disease or diabetes in the family?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Dad had a heart attack at about seventy. No diabetes in the family, far as I've heard. Mum's ninety-one and still attacking the crossword.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure's 152 over 88, pulse 78. Heart sounds are normal and regular, no murmur, and the lungs are clear.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Is 152 bad? And the tight feeling, what do you reckon that is?
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pressure's a bit up. The tightness might be angina brought on by effort, or it might just be you being unfit. I can't separate those two today.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Angina. That's a bit of a shock.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll get an ECG today, and bloods for cholesterol, kidney function and a sugar. They're booked before you leave.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): What if it keeps happening?
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it hasn't settled, we might do a scan, a CT of the arteries. Not today, only if it's still going. I'll see you in a fortnight with the results either way.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): And if it comes on and doesn't go when I stop?

[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it stays after you've rested, or you get proper pain, sweating, or it starts while you're sitting, ring an ambulance. Don't drive. Take the aspirin every morning, not just when you remember, and keep the perindopril going as you are.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Aspirin next to the kettle. See you in a fortnight. Sorry about the waffle.

spec.situation: Man or woman 50-70 who comes 'for a check-up' and only slowly admits a tight feeling in the chest when climbing stairs or walking fast; first denies chest pain, later describes the tightness. Takes a BP tablet and aspirin on and off. Doctor orders ECG and bloods.
features: patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

omissions.text: Exertional chest tightness occurs most times when the patient is rushing, not just occasionally.
The patient denied chest pain when asked directly.
The patient denied shortness of breath apart from being a bit puffed when rushing; no resting shortness of breath was reported.
Rosuvastatin was stopped in March because of severe muscle aches.
Ezetimibe was prescribed but the patient never filled the script and never took it.
ECG and blood tests were booked to be done before the patient leaves.
The follow-up in a fortnight is specifically to review the results.
